news.title: Spot gold hits over 14-month low amid Fed rate hike certainty, AI trade rout
Oil prices gain amid fears of renewed violence between U.S. and Iran
Gold at $3,625: five forces behind the sell-off, and four reasons buyers haven’t quit
body: Gold now trades below most major bank year-end targets, leaving it oversold on fundamentals but without a catalyst to turn it. With the $3,700 handle gone, traders are looking for support in the low $3,600s and high $3,500s, and a clean break would invite more momentum selling. The December 9 Fed decision is the main event risk: a 50 basis point hike or a higher dot plot would extend losses, while any hint the cycle is near its end could spark a sharp short-covering bounce. Miners are still far above record production costs, so margins can absorb further weakness, and supply is unlikely to tighten from producers cutting output.
Gold’s sellers have rates, yields and the dollar on their side, while its buyers are central banks and long-term investors who are patient but too slow to stop the slide.

Gold has slumped to around $3,625 an ounce, about 35% below its record near $5,590 set in late January. Sellers have been in control for most of the year, and the past week has brought some of the heaviest losses yet. The bull case has not disappeared, but it now rests on slower-moving, structural buyers, while the forces pushing prices down are immediate and tied to rates. Here is how the two sides line up.

The biggest weight on gold is the Federal Reserve. Minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all officials expect further hikes, markets see a December move as close to certain, and J.P. Morgan now forecasts hikes in December, January and March. Each step raises the cost of holding a metal that pays no yield. Hawkish signals from the Fed drove gold’s 3% slide this week, its steepest in some time.

The US 10-year Treasury yield is holding above 5%, and the dollar index is near its highest in about 19 months. Together they give investors a competitive return elsewhere and make gold more expensive for buyers outside the US.

Through the Middle East conflict, gold has not behaved as a haven. Escalation pushes oil higher, oil feeds inflation, and inflation feeds expectations of further Fed hikes and higher yields. Renewed US-Iran strikes this month brought no safe-haven buying, with rates outweighing geopolitics.

The outflows are concentrated in the US. North America was the only region with gold ETF outflows in October, and retail bar and coin demand fell about a fifth year on year in the third quarter. The weakness was most visible in Asia’s two biggest consumer markets. Indian bar and coin buying fell about 40%, accounting for most of the global drop, and jewellery demand in both China and India fell by around a fifth as high prices put shoppers off. Silver, down more than 60% from its peak, shows how hard forced selling has hit the wider precious metals complex.

Big banks have been lowering their numbers. Goldman Sachs has cut its outlook twice in less than a month, most recently trimming its end-2027 target to $4,650 from $4,800 after earlier reducing it from $5,400. On the charts, the break below $3,700 removed a closely watched level, and some analysts see the next support areas in the high $3,500s to mid-$3,600s.

The strongest argument for the bulls is official-sector demand. Central banks bought about 321 tonnes in the third quarter, up more than 40% on a year earlier. Goldman Sachs assumes roughly 60 tonnes a month of central bank buying, against about 17 tonnes before 2022, and sees that as the main pillar of its forecast. These purchases tend to show up in data with a lag, so they offer little near-term support for prices.

Global gold ETF holdings reached a record near 4,256 tonnes in October, helped by inflows from European funds. Chinese retail investors have also stayed committed: bar and coin demand in China rose 7% year on year in the third quarter, and its year-to-date total is the highest on record. That suggests the selling is regional rather than a wholesale exit from gold.

Even after the cuts, major bank forecasts are well above the current price. Goldman Sachs sees $4,650 by the end of 2027, Morgan Stanley targets $5,250 for the fourth quarter of 2027, and Deutsche Bank sees a conditional debasement case for 2027 to 2028 if the Fed eventually eases or financial repression returns. The gap between those targets largely reflects different assumptions about rates and official buying.

Gold’s best route back is the end of the hiking cycle. Goldman Sachs’s base case has the Fed cutting from the second half of 2027. Once markets start pricing an end to tightening, the main source of selling pressure would ease.

For now, the sellers. The forces pushing gold lower are fast-moving and tied to rates, while the buyers are patient, price-insensitive and slow to show up in the data. The next key test is the December 9 Fed decision and its projections, which will show how far into 2027 officials expect to keep hiking. Until the rate outlook turns, central bank demand looks more likely to slow the decline than reverse it.

news.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 19 Nov Inflation worries sink stocks
body: Inflation is still the concern. The Philly Fed survey showed manufacturers paying higher prices even as new orders slipped into contraction, and Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said inflation remains well above the Fed’s 2% target. That leaves the Fed facing persistent price pressure just as some of the activity and labor data are starting to soften. investinglive.com

Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut gave buyers an early reason to step in. The Nasdaq Composite was up more than 2% at its high and finished down 2.25%. Treasuries caught a bid as stocks fell, but the 10-year yield still ended the afternoon above 5%. The dollar firmed, gold and Bitcoin sold off, and the late crude quote held a gain as traders weighed shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. wsj.com

The USD was strongest against the Australian dollar and gained the least against the euro. AUDUSD fell 0.89% to 0.6657 after Australia’s unemployment rate rose to 4.9%. GBPUSD fell 0.49% to 1.3082, while USDJPY was up 0.22% at 159.68 after getting within four pips of 160.00. EURUSD slipped 0.04% to 1.0969. images.investinglive.com

The 2-year yield was up 3.4 basis points at the European close and down 3.4 basis points in late U.S. trading as flight to safety flows sent yields lower. The front end led the reversal as the stock selloff deepened. The 10-year was still above 5%, a level that keeps borrowing costs and stock valuations in focus. images.investinglive.com
The S&P 500 fell for a sixth straight session, with more than 90% of its members lower. Small caps were also down about 2% late in the day. apnews.com

Anthropic priced at $83, opened at $111.50 and reached $115.10 before closing at $97.17, up 17.1% from the offer price. The roughly $81 billion public offering drew strong demand, but the buying failed to carry through to the broader AI trade. AMD fell 7.7% to $489.19 after a Hunterbrook report raised questions about its exposure to U.S. chip export controls on China. images.investinglive.com

The November Philly Fed index fell to 6.3 from 20.9, well below the 20.0 estimate. New orders dropped to −0.4, while prices paid jumped to 58.2 from 43.2, the highest since April. Initial jobless claims edged up to 203K versus 197K expected. The bigger move was in continuing claims, which rose 70K to 1.763 million, suggesting people already out of work may be taking longer to find a job. investinglive.com

Goolsbee described the labor market as stable and consumer demand as solid. He also said tariffs have had a more persistent effect than expected and pointed to the war as another source of inflation. Those remarks kept the focus on price pressure a day after Waller raised the possibility of a 50-basis-point hike in December. Separately, InvestingLive reported, citing CBC, that Canada is seeking an interim U.S. tariff deal by year-end covering sectors including steel, aluminum, autos and lumber. images.investinglive.com

The late U.S. crude quote was $83.99, up $0.73 or 0.88%. December WTI futures officially settled at $83.21, down $0.05. Reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz offered support, while rising U.S. inventories and expectations of a global surplus limited the move. Further disruption would keep energy prices in the Fed’s inflation discussion.

Gold fell 2.69% to $3,624.74, and silver dropped 4.71% to $42.922. The firmer dollar was a headwind, and the late decline in Treasury yields did little to cushion the metals. Copper also fell 1.40% to $5.5890, consistent with caution about industrial demand. Bitcoin slipped 2.20% to $61,592, moving with equities as the early appetite for risk faded.

The next session will show whether buyers can hold a rebound after Thursday’s reversal. The 10-year yield above 5%, Anthropic’s ability to hold its first-day gains and any fresh disruption in Hormuz are the levels and headlines to watch. The Fed’s challenge remains the same. Price pressures are proving persistent while parts of the economy are losing momentum.

news.title: J.P. Morgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call
body: A tier-one house moving from one more hike to three adds weight to the view that tightening doesn’t end in December, which supports two-year Treasury yields and the dollar. Pricing for 2027 is now where the action is, so January and March contracts are likely to firm. Strength against the yen is limited by a likely BoJ hike and intervention risk near 160. A Fed with no clear story to justify a pause makes every inflation release a market event, including any knock-on effects from oil.
J.P. Morgan has dropped its “December and done” view: it now expects three straight hikes, with the Fed defending its credibility rather than reacting to a hot labour market.

J.P. Morgan has moved to a longer Fed tightening path, now forecasting quarter-point rate hikes in January and March 2027 on top of the December increase it already expected. If all three go ahead, the federal funds target range would rise from 3.75% to 4.00% now to 4.50% to 4.75% by March. The new path would mean hikes at the December 8 to 9, January 26 to 27 and March 16 to 17 meetings.

The bank’s economists, led by chief US economist Michael Feroli, said the extra hikes are not meant to weaken the labour market, which they argue has not been a source of inflation. The aim instead is to protect the Fed’s credibility when policymakers have no convincing reason to stop. In their view, sticky inflation keeps the case for further tightening alive.

The revision is a notable change of view. As recently as early October, J.P. Morgan expected December to be the last move of the cycle. It argued then that supply shocks were the main driver of inflation and would not justify a long campaign into 2027. Adding two more hikes suggests the bank no longer sees price pressure as a passing supply story.

The economists also raised a point about communication under Chair Kevin Warsh. They said the Fed has not set out an overarching narrative for its policy path, and without one, decisions are more likely to react to each new data release. In practice, that raises the stakes for every inflation release between now and March.

The call fits the tone of the Fed’s own minutes. The record of the October 27 to 28 meeting, released on Wednesday, showed almost all officials judged further hikes would likely be needed if the economy evolved as they expected. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee added to that on Thursday, saying that in his view a sizeable part of inflation comes from demand, not just oil and tariff shocks.

J.P. Morgan is not alone. Deutsche Bank and Bank of America also forecast hikes at three straight meetings, while Goldman Sachs and UBS expect a shorter path after December and some other forecasters see a longer pause. Markets price a quarter-point December hike as close to certain, with a small chance of a half-point move. The bigger question now is whether the cycle ends in December or runs well into 2027, and J.P. Morgan has clearly taken the second view.

news.title: More from Fed’s Goolsbee: AI boom a ‘pig through the python’ that risks overheating US economy
body: Goolsbee’s remarks add a demand-side argument to a Fed debate already leaning toward hikes. Markets heavily favour a quarter-point move on December 9, and a voice outside the usual hawks warning of overheating supports front-end yields and the dollar. He says inflation is not just an oil and tariff story, so a pullback in crude would ease less of the pressure than traders might hope. His uncertainty about how banks would cope with an AI-led equity correction marks a tail risk for stocks that could quickly reverse the tightening narrative.
Goolsbee says the AI boom has become an inflation problem, with investment and stock market wealth pushing on an economy that may not have the room to absorb them.

Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee warned on Thursday that the artificial intelligence boom is adding to the risk of the US economy overheating. Business investment at near-unprecedented levels may be more than the economy’s capacity can absorb, he argued. He compared the surge to a pig moving through a python and said he found it hard to see the AI boom as anything other than a contributor to overheating. He made the comments in a call with reporters on the day Anthropic set a record for an initial public offering.

Goolsbee’s central message was that he does not yet see inflation on a path back to the Fed’s 2% target. In his view, inflation has proved far more persistent than expected in 2025, and recent months have not brought good news. He called the level of inflation borderline disturbingly high and said how steep the rate path needs to be depends on whether inflation is seen returning to target.

He was explicit that the pressure is not only coming from supply shocks. Oil and tariffs have played a part, he said, but there is also a sizeable demand component. That is why he is watching services inflation closely, as a guide to whether price pressures come from demand or from costs such as energy.

He pointed to two channels through which AI is shaping the economy: investment, and the wealth effect from rising equity values. The Anthropic listing raises the question of how shareholders will spend their gains, he said, which could have a broader macroeconomic impact. He added that businesses widely acknowledge costs are rising, especially in construction and at firms competing with data centres for components.

Not every signal was hawkish. Goolsbee said he is not concerned about wages pushing up inflation at this point. He described consumer spending as broad-based and financed mostly by income growth. He was less certain about the risks around equities. It is unclear how the financial sector would fare in a major AI-related stock correction, he said, and he is unsure whether fallout from the US midterm elections will slow the data centre buildout or leave a lasting mark on share prices. He also said greater openness about monetary policy has been productive for the Fed and for the world.

The remarks add a new strand to the Fed’s debate ahead of the December 8 to 9 meeting, where hikes are the focus. Minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all participants saw further hikes as likely appropriate, and markets lean heavily toward a quarter-point rise from the current 3.75% to 4.00% range. Goolsbee, a 2027 voter, did not commit to the size of a December move in the remarks available. But by framing AI as a demand-side inflation risk, he gives the hawks another argument. If services inflation and investment spending stay hot into early 2027, a longer tightening cycle looks more likely than a quick finish.

news.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Friday, November 20, 2026: Fed's Paulson, Japan CPI and China’s LPR
body: USD/JPY near 160 is where today’s events meet. A firm Japan CPI would support the yen at the margin, but a Fed that is also hiking limits how far the rate gap can narrow, and intervention warnings near 160 cap the upside. If Paulson sounds open to a 50 basis point move rather than gradual steps, front-end Treasury yields and the dollar would likely rise. Energy is a big part of Japan’s inflation pickup, so oil prices feed straight into the BoJ’s thinking. A hold on the LPR should barely move the yuan, while a surprise cut would stand out given the overnight-rate overhaul.
Two hawkish central banks get fresh tests in the Asian session, while China’s loan prime rate holds as a benchmark the PBoC has quietly moved past.

The Asian session brings a cluster of events that will test how firmly markets are leaning into a global tightening story. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson speaks late in the US day, Japan’s national inflation figures for October are released at the same time, and China’s monthly loan prime rate fixing follows early in the session. The first two fit squarely into a hawkish narrative on both sides of the Pacific. The third is a largely procedural event that matters less than it used to.
Fed’s Paulson: a 2026 voter on a committee leaning toward hikes

Paulson is due to speak at 23:30 GMT (18:30 US Eastern) at a Money Marketeers of New York University dinner in New York. She is scheduled to address communications and monetary policy, and a speech text and a question-and-answer session are expected. As a 2026 FOMC voter, her views carry weight heading into the December 8 to 9 meeting, with the decision due on December 9.

Her recent record is clear. In a speech earlier this month she said further gradual rate increases seemed appropriate. Policy needs to be somewhat restrictive to get inflation back to 2%, she said, and underlying inflation appears stuck between 2.5% and 3%. She would favour moving faster if inflation expectations drift higher, wage pressures build or underlying inflation rises. She backed the September hike and the October hold.

The backdrop has grown more hawkish since then. Minutes of the October 27 to 28 meeting, released on Wednesday, showed nearly all participants judged that further increases in the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate in the coming months. Governor Christopher Waller believes officials should consider a half-point move in December, arguing that recent inflation is heading the wrong way. With the target range at 3.75% to 4.00%, markets lean heavily toward a quarter-point hike. Deutsche Bank expects hikes in December, January and March, while Citigroup sees a 25 basis point move in December with a higher risk of 50.
The key question for Paulson is whether she sticks with “gradual” or shows any openness to the larger step Waller has floated. Any change in how she talks about the pace would make the headline.
Japan’s October CPI: inflation data ahead of a likely BoJ hike

Japan’s national CPI for October is due at 23:30 GMT (18:30 US Eastern). The consensus for the core measure, which excludes fresh food, is 2.3%, up from 2.1% in September. The prior headline reading was 2.1%, and the measure excluding both fresh food and energy was 2.4%. Economists have linked much of the recent pickup to higher energy costs from the Middle East conflict reaching household bills, while a weak yen has pushed up import prices.

The data arrive with the Bank of Japan in a hawkish mood. The policy rate is 1.25% after a hike in September, its highest in 31 years. On Thursday, Governor Kazuo Ueda said the bank expects to keep raising rates because monetary conditions remain accommodative. He also flagged an upside risk that underlying inflation could overshoot the 2% target. A Reuters poll shows 86% of economists expect a hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting, which would be a third increase this year. Nearly 60% look for a further move to 1.75% by the end of March. Producer prices strengthened the case earlier this month, rising 7.1% y/y in October, ahead of forecasts.

There are complications. The economy unexpectedly contracted in the July to September quarter, and the yen is trading near 160 per dollar despite heavy intervention this year. A firm CPI reading would reinforce December hike pricing. A soft one would give doves a talking point, though probably not enough to derail the move given Ueda’s latest remarks.
PBoC loan prime rates: an 18th hold expected for a fading benchmark

China’s loan prime rates are due at 01:15 GMT (20:15 US Eastern). In a Reuters survey of 28 market participants, 23 expect the one-year LPR to hold at 3.0% and the five-year at 3.5%. That would be an 18th consecutive month unchanged. Five respondents see a cut to one or both rates, the first break from unanimous no-change forecasts in recent months. Citigroup analysts see a November cut as implausible and expect rates to stay on hold through 2026, followed by two 10 basis point cuts in 2027.

news.title: Fed’s Goolsbee says he sees no clear path back to 2% inflation
body: Goolsbee’s comments on inflation, interest rates and AI investment crossed the wires.

The takeaway is hawkish. Goolsbee sees a sizable demand component to inflation, which makes it harder for the Fed to look through the recent price pressure. Businesses are already reporting higher costs where they compete with data centers for components, and he sees a risk that the economy has trouble absorbing the current pace of investment without overheating.

Services inflation is the barometer to watch. If it stays sticky even as energy pressures ease, that would strengthen the case that demand is keeping inflation elevated and give the Fed more reason to tighten. If services inflation cools, the case for a steeper rate path weakens.

news.title: AUDUSD moves to a new low.   Price action is ping ponging down and up and back down again.
body: Australia’s October jobs report was considerably weaker than expected. Employment fell 43,500 against the 25,500 gain expected in our preview, and the unemployment rate rose to 4.9% versus 4.7% expected. September’s job loss was revised to 36,400 from 39,300, putting the two-month decline at nearly 80,000 jobs, the biggest in five years.

The rise in unemployment alongside a drop in participation is the detail that stands out. A smaller share of Australians were working or looking for work, and even with that decline in participation, more people were unemployed. The ABS’s smoothed trend measure still showed a modest gain of 7,200 jobs, but trend unemployment also rose, to 4.8%.

The RBA raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% earlier this month and warned that inflation would stay elevated for longer. The jobs report strengthens the case for a hold on December 8. Reuters reported that traders unwound bets on further hikes and priced in roughly 45 basis points of easing by the end of 2027, about double what they had priced before the release

The AUDUSD initially fell sharply from 0.67202 to near 0.6660 after the weaker-than-expected Australian jobs report. Buyers came back in and erased nearly the entire decline, taking the pair back toward the Asian session high at 0.6720 early in North American trading.

That rebound did not last. As U.S. stocks reversed their early gains, traders turned their attention back to U.S. inflation concerns and still-solid jobs data. Sellers took control again, retracing the entire bounce and extending the move to a new session low at 0.66562. The pair is trading at 0.66624 as the North American session winds down.

The session low at 0.66562 dipped just below the 200-week moving average at 0.66575. The price is back above it for now, putting the focus on where the pair closes the week. A weekly close below 0.66575 would give sellers more control and increase the potential for further downside.

If buyers can hold above that moving average and build on the bounce, the 100-week moving average at 0.67043 is the first key topside target. Getting back above it would give buyers more room to make a run at the session high near 0.6720.

news.title: Peterson: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means
body: Artificial intelligence is about to sweep through the economy. The Federal Reserve is bracing for impact.

"We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear.

The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses, but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed.

With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. AI lab Anthropic plans to price the shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to contemplate raising interest rates in December to slow down the rate of price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy.

Meanwhile Americans are souring on some aspects of the technology. The Nov. 3 midterms saw voters enact an array of state-level measures to slow down construction of the data centers that are essential to powering AI.

Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend.

It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of Commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island.
Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said.
Warsh didn't say whether he shares that view, and how it would translate into monetary policy isn't exactly clear.

The event was an unusual one for the Fed. The central bank employs a small army of Ph.D. economists who can rapidly weigh in on anything affecting the U.S. and global economies. But in keeping with his long-standing critiques of the Fed as insular and outdated, Warsh has chosen to draw expertise from outside the institution to help it figure out how to think about what AI will do to productivity and jobs.
Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking.

The public heard Monday from one of the three official members of the task force: venture capitalist Marc Andreessen. Warsh went to Stanford University with Andreessen's wife, and the two have been longtime friends. Another task force member, Stanford economist Chad Jones, is on leave and working at Anthropic and couldn't speak during the company's blackout period ahead of the IPO. The third, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, didn't attend the event.

Andreessen is hugely optimistic about the promise of AI as a technology, but believes the government won't let Americans experience its full effects. Heavy regulation in areas such as healthcare and education mean technology can't replace people's jobs in those sectors, he said.

"To the extent our economy is a free market economy, then maybe you could see the, let's say, extremely rapid displacement scenarios people are talking about," Andreessen said. "But we've mostly outlawed the kind of job transition that … both the utopians the doomers talk about."
